title: Texas RB Hollywood Smothers surprisingly added to injury report, questionable vs. Tennessee
description: Smothers scored the game-winning touchdown against Ohio State two weeks ago.
fullText:
The first injury report for this weekend's clash between No. 1 Texas and No. 14 Tennessee came with a bit of a surprise.

Texas starting running back Hollywood Smothers has been ruled questionable for the game, in addition to defensive lineman Justus Terry, defensive back Xavier Filsaime and offensive lineman Jordan Coleman all being ruled out. Tight end Nick Townsend is also doubtful.

Per On3, Smothers is dealing with a lower body injury and his availability will be decided based on how the week progresses.

Smothers joined Steve Sarkisian's program this season after two years at North Carolina State. He's had a successful start with the Longhorns, logging 198 rushing yards on 41 carries, 54 receiving yards and three total touchdowns in three games for the undefeated team.

That included the game-winning leap in Texas' epic comeback win against then-No. 1 Ohio State.

If Smothers is unable to play, Raleek Brown has posted the second-most carries on the team with 31, which he has turned into 129 rushing yards and two touchdowns. Freshmen Derrek Cooper and Michael Terry III are the only other runners on the team with double-digit carries.

title: How the Cubs Playoff Rotation is Shaping Up
description: With the MLB postseason race shaping up, the Chicago Cubs' playoff rotation is becoming clearer. They have occasionally had a rough time with their pitching staff this season, and it has been hard to know who they can trust. However, they are heading for a best-of-three series in the Wild Card round. This means that …
fullText:
With the MLB postseason race shaping up, the Chicago Cubs' playoff rotation is becoming clearer. They have occasionally had a rough time with their pitching staff this season, and it has been hard to know who they can trust. However, they are heading for a best-of-three series in the Wild Card round. This means that they need to start figuring out which three starters make the cut.

Clay Holmes feels safely locked into being one of the three pitchers in the Cubs playoff rotation. Chicago made a massive trade to acquire Holmes at the deadline. Since he returned from injury, it has been worth the cost. He is one of the key players for the Cubs' run in October.

Although his 4.26 ERA is not amazing, it does not tell the full story. He had a strong stretch before struggling in the past three starts, allowing 16 earned runs. This makes it a little concerning, but before that he was rock solid and one of the team's best starters. In four starts before, he allowed only one run. His ability to force ground balls fits in perfectly with the Cubs' elite defense.

Now, the Cubs could play it safe with Holmes and limit his usage over the final week of the regular season. He would be set for one final start, where it may help to play him to get things right. It may be too long of a gap between games, so it would be a surprise if he does not at least pitch a few innings in a game. Before his struggles, it looked like he would be a possible game one starter. Even if he does not get that role, it feels highly unlikely that he does not get a postseason start.

One of the other big trade deadline additions was Kevin Gausman. He is the most experienced pitcher for Chicago, appearing in plenty of postseason games. Since coming to the team, he has given the team good length. Additionally, Chicago has won a majority of his starts.

Heading into his September 23rd start against the Marlins, he has a rough 5.04 ERA with the Cubs. However, like Holmes, that has been inflated by rough games. Gausman is still 4-2 in 44 2/3 innings pitched. His ability to go deep into games is needed with Chicago's rough bullpen. There is a possibility that he is not in the Cubs playoff rotation for the wild card round. Although his experience and durability make it hard not to rely on him.

The third spot is where it gets tricky. Technically, this spot is not guaranteed. If either team wins both of the first two games, the series wouldn't need a third starter. However, if Chicago advanced, the Cubs playoff rotation would be expanded. With this in mind, Matthew Boyd would likely be in the Cubs playoff rotation for the first round.

Boyd has been a reliable option for Chicago this year when he has stayed healthy. He is 9-5 with a 4.06 ERA. The veteran lefty also has plenty of experience at Wrigley Field. If Chicago secures the top Wild Card spot, this would be an advantage. He could very well start either of the first two games as well. The only pitcher possibly above him in the order is Holmes. Boyd and Gausman could come down to which team they face and how they fare against the veteran pitchers.

Shota Imanaga and David Peterson are also hanging around for a possible start. Imanaga is hard to trust with his home run issue, but has seemed to stabilize himself. Peterson is stringing together good starts, and he could very well start in the playoffs. All of the pitchers have question marks around them, but these two may have fewer answers.

When looking at the Cubs playoff rotation, there are multiple ways Chicago can go. All of the starters have shown flashes, but also had very rough games. They still have a week to go, and the decision could be impacted by their opponent. Holmes, Gausman, and Boyd have seemed to separate themselves a bit. Regardless of who gets which game, they will need to set the tone for the series, as it is nearly impossible to trust the bullpen.

title: A Key Safety Feature Shipped in the May OpenTofu Release
description: Dynamic prevent_destroy values make it easier to manage resources like databases with IaC.
fullText:
OpenTofu v1.12.0 was released in May and of the new functionality, there is one that sticks out as worth mentioning: dynamic lifecycle.prevent_destroy.

Before this release, prevent_destroy had to be a static value. Which meant if you wanted destroy protection on your prod instance but not on dev and staging instances of the same root module, you needed to jump through some hoops.

Now prevent_destroy can be defined dynamically so a Multi-Instance root module can do this:

prevent_destroy = var.prevent_destroy_enabled

Your prod root module instance can now set prevent_destroy_enabled = true. Dev and ephemeral instances can default it to false and tear down freely without intervention.

This is a UX improvement I love to see because it makes safety easy. Particularly when we've seen big clients who manage lots of databases be spooked by managing DBs via IaC (suffering from fear of resource deletion), this feels like it'll calm nerves and help adoption (even if only slightly).

Also worth a look in this release: the new destroy = false lifecycle option, which removes a resource from state without destroying the real infrastructure. Another nice safety lever for day-2 ops!

The OpenTofu team keeps shipping and I'm a fan!

title: Australia says OpenAI agent hacked into government website
description: The OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to public and non-public files in what could be the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website.
fullText:
The OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to public and non-public files in what could be the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website.

SYDNEY: Australia said on Wednesday (Sep 23) an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorised access to files, in what could be the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website.

The breach is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing external systems outside the United States, coming on top of several recent breaches globally by rogue AI agents that have alarmed governments and companies.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the medical statistics portal of a government agency responsible for non-sensitive health data and statistics, including public medical spending.

"Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the ... network. Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable," Albanese said during a media briefing in New York, where he is attending the UN General Assembly.

Investigations continue and Australia had voiced its "extreme concern about this incident" to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Albanese said, adding that he was deeply disappointed by the company's delay in notifying the government.

"It took until Sep 10 before there was any notification at all," Albanese said, adding that the investigation would also examine why government systems had failed to detect the breach in the first place.

He also warned that three other government websites "may be impacted" by the OpenAI agent's activity.

"The question is, when it was trying to harvest data, did it go into these other sites? So we're not confirming that that occurred," he said.

The incident comes after OpenAI and Anthropic, in separate submissions to a parliamentary inquiry this month, urged Australia to reconsider a ban preventing them from using the country's creative content to train their models.

"Our review found no evidence of patient records being accessed. The information accessed included aggregate health statistics and internal file names," OpenAI said in a statement.

It added that it "identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers ... our models took actions we did not intend".The breach is one of several recent incidents in which OpenAI has disclosed hacks or unauthorised activity involving its AI agents well after they occurred.

In some cases this was because the activity was only detected belatedly, and in others because the company initially elected not to disclose it.

A separate high-profile incident, a mid-July intrusion into open-source AI repository Hugging Face, was only detected about a week after it took place, according to timelines released by OpenAI and independent investigators.

This helped ignite a global conversation about the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI models.

Rivals Anthropic, Google's Gemini, and Meta have also disclosed incidents of their agents accessing external systems.

Some of America's top AI executives, including Altman, have called for a slowdown of AI development, citing, among other things, the threat of devastating cyberattacks by out-of-control agents.

title: The Death of Reading (With James Marriott) [audio]
description: Are we living in the new Dark Ages? Despite vast technological advances, our societies are increasingly looking like those that preceded the advent of literacy. So argues journalist James Marriott, who sees in our abandonment of reading a threat to democracy and a reversal of many of the Enlightenment’s gains. He and EconTalk’s Russ Roberts […]
fullText:
Intro. [Recording date: August 16, 2026.]

Russ Roberts: Today is August 16th, 2026, and my guest is author James Marriott of the Times of London, where he is a columnist. His Substack is Cultural Capital. He was first here in July of 2025, talking about reading. Today, we're going to talk about his new book, The New Dark Ages: The Death of Reading and the Dawn of the Post-Literate Society. James, welcome back to EconTalk.

James Marriott: Thanks so much for having me. It's actually, amazingly, I talked to you last in the middle of a sweltering London heatwave, and I'm in the middle of another sweltering London heatwave, although it's less hot. When I looked back at that video, I'm completely pink in the last time I talked to you.

Russ Roberts: Well, we'll have to do this more often. Or it's a tradition.

Russ Roberts: It's pretty dark to call a book The New Dark Ages. Is the situation really that bleak?

James Marriott: Yeah, it's a funny one. It's a title that--my publisher said, 'What are you calling this book?' And, you know, something just springs into your mind, and you say it before you thought about it, and I just said, 'Well, The New Dark Ages.' And then, it got attached to the project.

And then, people have asked me, 'Well, do you think we're literally returning to the dark ages? Is it really true that a society with self-driving cars and world-beating research universities is remotely comparable to the situation of Europe in the fifth or sixth century or whatever?' That's not the argument of the book. I mean, the other objection people make is: aren't you caricaturing the dark ages, which is, historians now tell us, were a time of great technological innovation, which I think is a bit overdone at the moment. But no, that's not what I'm doing either.

I guess the thought behind the title comes from a fairly common idea among the kinds of media theorists who've written about the implications of moving from a society based on literacy and reading to one that abandons literacy and reading and begins to look a little bit more, in some ways, like the kinds of societies that preceded the advent of literacy.

We owe Marshall McLuhan this idea that a post-literate society will resemble, in some ways, a pre-literate society. The things I sort of say in my book and the things people like Marshall McLuhan and Walter Ong would say is more mystical, more emotional, more face-to-face interaction, not mediated by the written word. So, I guess the thing the title is pointing at is this sort of well-known thought in media-theoretical circles that a society after literacy, in some ways, resembles a society before literacy.

And, I try not to press too hard on the historical parallels. You may think I've overdone it, but I guess if the book has two themes, it's the idea that the decline of literacy may push us back through a kind of reversal of many of the gains of the Enlightenment, which I think was a sort of phenomenon symptom of literacy, and also that it may push us back to a political situation that resembles one that existed before literacy. So, I guess the theme is slightly going back in time to a time before literacy.

Russ Roberts: I'm not sure I agree or disagree. I think it's a really interesting idea to think about. And your book starts with a really interesting--it's a very short book, by the way. I want to tell listeners. It's about 170 pages on my Kindle. I ironically read it on my phone. We'll talk about that later, maybe. But, your book starts off with, really, a history of reading, and I've never thought about the question of: when did reading become common? When did literacy become common? So, when did reading take off?

James Marriott: It's a really good question. And I think this is something I really wanted to hammer home in the book, which is that I think we're so used to reading, we're so used to literacy, and it's so ubiquitous in our society, and we spend our entire lives reading, that we very easily forget to think about how unusual it is and how recent it is.

So, the statistics of literacy rates in ancient societies are fascinating. By some estimates, in ancient Mesopotamia, I think in the Mesopotamian city-state, you might have had 20 people alive who could read and write. The early history of literacy for thousands and thousands of years is incredibly fragile, and it's not at all a cultural phenomenon. It's a kind of esoteric elite code or secret that's passed down among a wealthy scribal elite. And, some rulers in some societies would have learned to read; some wouldn't.

That's the situation that prevails. I mean, in ancient Rome, the literacy rate is probably about 10%. It's edging up a little bit by the end of the Middle Ages.

The obvious big event for literacy is the invention of the printing press, which means that books can proliferate enormously. When people have more access to books, more people can read; books become useful for more things. Driven by Protestantism, a strand of Christianity which places a huge emphasis on the written word, more people become literate to read the Bible. And, one story of literacy is that these things interrelate and feed each other up until the middle to the end of the 18th century, when there's this phenomenon that's called the Reading Revolution by some historians, which is this idea that reading has sort of been increasing steadily since the printing press, and you reach this point in the middle to the end of the 18th century where it suddenly seems, as numerous journalists and authors were writing at the time, that absolutely everybody is reading.

And there are all these wonderful accounts of people complaining that you can be walking in the street and the people walking down, bumping into you because they're reading a novel. Or, you go to the pub and there are just loads of peasants sitting there reading almanacs, or you go and see what earth your servant girl is doing, and she's in the kitchen reading a newspaper.

And, journalists are always prone to exaggeration, but it really did seem to strike people at the time that there was this point in the middle to the end of the 18th century when it seemed like not many people had been reading, and then suddenly everybody was reading, and books were everywhere, and magazines were everywhere, and newspapers were everywhere. And, if you're going to find an inflection point, that's not mass literacy, but I think that is the beginning of this modern literate world that we know.

Russ Roberts: We did an episode with Janine Barchas on inexpensive paperbacks and Jane Austen and how the widespread availability of affordable books launched the popularity of a whole bunch of people, one of whom was Jane Austen.

One of the challenges, I think, with this claim that reading is important--by the way, you and I share something in common. We love books. We read, I think, an enormous amount. We spent an enormous amount of our life--I'm older than you, but I've spent a huge part of my life immersed in a book, reading in times where I should have been watching where I was going. So, I totally--we're on the same page there.

But the question that's hovering in the background of this book and that comes forward in the last part is whether it matters to civilization, whether it matters to our political process.

Certainly, it should, on paper. It should be the case that a literate population should make better decisions, you would think, you would hope. But, I'd have to say that if I think back to this revolution, which was a big deal, it wasn't like a 20% increase in people reading books or a 10% increase. It was an enormous increase, again, mainly through the printing press and the fall in the price of owning a book and access to books. Shouldn't the world have looked radically different? And, you try to make the case that it did, but I'm skeptical. So, make that case again. It should have been a revolution in how the world turned out. It should have been almost visible in political outcomes. And, I'm not sure it is. So, give me your best shot.

James Marriott: Yeah. I mean, I wouldn't go so far as to claim that literacy is the only factor that matters in the history of politics. I think it does look pretty radical.

For instance, I think the important thing to say about literacy, perhaps, is that I think the more literacy spreads through society, the more of a democratizing effect that has on the society. The more people who can access information and ideas, the more people can become politically involved, and the more people are thinking critically about power. And, it used to be the case that historians would claim that the French Revolution was basically a consequence of philosophers like Rousseau publishing their anti-monarchical and proto-Republican ideas in books like The Social Contract. That's probably overstated, but I think if you look at the history of--in Britain, perhaps more you're talking about the end of the 17th century. In Europe, you're talking about the 18th century.

You begin the 18th century, in which Europe is a society run, to a very large degree, by absolutist monarchs who have total power of their populations, surrounded by ministers. Political affairs are basically palace secret, discussed by a small minority of a political elite.

When you get to the end of the 18th century and the beginning of the 19th century, society is looking a lot more democratic. You have newspapers. The phenomena of the absolutist monarch is radically waned. In France, you have a republic. In England, the monarch is much less the sole authority in the country than they were at the beginning of the century. You have reports of Parliament being written; ordinary people involved in politics; public affairs are no longer just debated in state rooms. There's a kind of collective decision made by the public sphere.

And, I do think politics really looks radically different. I think that sort of end of the 18th century, beginning of the 19th century is a great age of democratic revolution and democratic reform, and I think that is directly linked to the spread of literacy through society.

Russ Roberts: Well, it could be there's a sweet spot. It could be it's a U-shaped or an inverted U-shaped function.

So, for example, you mentioned The Social Contract. Thomas Paine gets a lot of credit for influencing the American Revolution. We could think of many, many books--Uncle Tom's Cabin--that electrified the public and led to important movements, although it's hard to know whether those claims are true, but certainly there's a plausibility to it.

The problem I have--and it's the same issue with the Internet. The Internet has democratized information beyond imagining and beyond what books could be, and, of course, the problem is, is that half of what's on the Internet is wrong; you just don't know which half. And the same would be true of books. And you can see this--and, by the way, I don't want to have listeners think this book is a--it is a bit of a screed, although I don't think James Marriott is capable of a real screed--meaning you're making the case for something, is the way I would put it.

But, the problem, of course, is that there's a lot of bad books, and there's a lot of books that are lies, and there are books that encourage people to do awful things. So, I can imagine that in the early days of literacy, when there was limited access to publishing books, some of the best books got published, we would hope, and they were very provocative and influential. Eventually, it got so democratized--and I'm not criticizing democracy, I just mean that there was a lot more available to a lot more people--it's a pretty mixed bag. I mean, I think you'd have trouble defending the idea that the Internet is leading to better political outcomes because people have more information. They do have more information, just not so reliable.

James Marriott: Yeah. No, I agree, and I think--I mean, this book is a bit of a polemic. I guess my argument would not be that--

Russ Roberts: That's a nice word. That's a better word. Sorry. It's not a screed.

James Marriott: Well, jeremiad is the thing that it has also being called.

I guess my argument with that would be I'm not at all saying that books are perfect and not at all saying that every book has a benign influence. My argument would be that the way that books structure information and present us with a picture of the world is fundamentally more rational and more coherent and more intelligent than the picture of information that you get if you are just talking to someone or if you're watching a video or a TikTok or, God forbid, even listen to a podcast.

I mean, there are various arguments that have made about this. When we write, we're forced to consider our ideas more carefully. You can go back and refine your ideas until you've thought of the best version of what you want to say. Writing allows you to externalize a part of your mind. So, you put your idea in the paper, you see how it stands up, you go back, and you refine it.

Readers, when you're given a written text, you have the ideas of the author fixed in front of you, so you can submit them to greater critical analysis. You can think about them more; you can reread them more.

I think all this stuff is harder to do in conversation or over video. Writers can't bypass logical argument through things like charm or shouting at somebody you disagree with or crying to persuade someone that you're being so horrifically mistreated, you should believe me, even though my argument isn't logical. So, the range of illogical appeals is much more restricted in the book than it is in person or in a video.

And I think these things don't make books perfect, but they mean that books tend to make more rational arguments about the world. I guess my other point would be, I think every argument has to stand up to its reductio ad Hitler. Someone will inevitably bring the Nazis--

Russ Roberts: I was thinking about it, yeah. I was thinking about Mein Kampf.

James Marriott: Well, exactly. I mean, my argument there would be that you could say there are two very famous arguments made for Nazism, perhaps, in different forms of media. One is Mein Kampf, the book that Hitler wrote--the semi-autobiographical, mad, illogical, rambling, deranged book that he wrote. And the other is the Leni Riefenstahl film, The Triumph of the Will. Mein Kampf was found unreadable even by senior Nazis. You have letters from senior Nazi saying, 'Oh my God, this book is awful. I can't be bothered to read it.' And although millions of copies were sold of Mein Kampf, there's good evidence that very few Germans ever managed to get through that book to the end, because Nazism, when you attempt to present it coherently in the form of a written text, makes no sense at all, and nobody wants to hear about it. And, it's just hard to fit that terrible idea into the logical argument that's required of a book, I would say.

The other argument for Nazism, Leni Riefenstahl's film, The Triumph of the Will, is--we wouldn't agree with it politically, but it's often regarded as an artistic masterpiece, and it's shown on university film courses, and that's a film that is thought to make a very powerful argument for Fascism.

And, I guess the comparison there would be that a bad idea translates much better into a film than it does into a book. It's very fun to hear someone becoming angry in person. We love watching arguments, and we love watching debates, and we love watching rhetorical showmanship and people flinging insults at one another.

That's really boring to read in a book eventually. As I say, with an opinion column, what with 900 words of invective might be interesting, if I just ranted at you for the length of a book, it would be really tedious, and therefore we tend not to do it. And, yeah--as I say, we just mustn't forget how much of what we value in our public discourse and have valued is almost unnatural to human communication. And, what we valued is this strange, impersonal thing that writing gave us and that we're now losing.

Russ Roberts: So, I want to digress for a second, or what seems like a digression. It's not. There's an extraordinary podcast called The History of Rock and Roll in 500 Songs. It's produced by Andrew Hickey. If you don't know it or haven't heard it and you care about music from popular music anytime from the 1950s on, you will find it extraordinary. And, he says something in there that blew me away--that you also say, which is--there's a four-part series that goes for seven or eight hours, I think, on "Sympathy for the Devil," the Rolling Stones song. And he says, 'Well, Jagger was reading this book called The Master and Margarita by Bulgakov.' And, if you've read the Master and Margarita, it opens with two Russian intellectuals poo-pooing the existence of God and making fun of belief and faith. And suddenly this suave gentleman shows up, and we come to realize--they think he's crazy at first--but we come to realize it's Satan. It's the devil, and he knows some things they don't know, and they have a comeuppance. It's a brilliant opening of the book.

But, that's the opening of "Sympathy for the Devil," where Jagger sings, 'Please allow me to introduce myself. I'm a man of wealth and taste.' And, he took that right out of The Master and Margarita, which is a pretty obscure novel.

And, you argue that Paul McCartney and many other great songwriters were great readers. They were influenced by--and Andrew Hickey in his podcast has many, many examples--and some of the great lyrics of a very different medium, popular music, were influenced by reading books. And, if we lose that, our songs will be less interesting.

James Marriott: That's an annoyingly good example that I wish I'd managed to put in my book. Maybe this later edition we can include it.

Yeah. I mean, I guess this is another point that I make of what literacy gives us as a culture, which is, I think, all the things that we've spoken about: the richness of books, the detail of books, the complexity of books, I think, informs a whole society, and it's not always immediately apparent that it's doing that, but it's often there providing, I think, a level of richness and nuance to all other kinds of cultural media that we might not think of. I mean, I gave the example of pop music specifically because it's so unlikely.

I mean, it can be taken too far. As I say in the book, I'm not suggesting that if you want to be in a boy band, take your pile of Penguin classics down to the British library and get reading. But I think it is very striking that so many great popular musicians and so many great popular songs are informed by books and are informed by reading. Bob Dylan, the obvious example of a great reader. Paul McCartney, the obvious example of a great reader.

And I just think any art that is rooted in the richness and complexity of reading will tend to give you a richer, deeper, more complex understanding of the world. And I use the example of pop music, as I say, because no one really thinks of pop music as a particularly literate genre. And, those musicians are probably also singing for a more literate population that was more accustomed to enjoying complex thoughts and complex ideas and complex feelings.

And, this is amazing research. I'm not going to be able to remember the figure off the top of my head that finds that in the last 20 years, pop songs have become less lyrically complex and less melodically complex. And, that's not entirely just because everybody has stopped reading books. It's also because the environment that we are entering is one that favors simplicity, immediacy, isn't very good at following a long and unfailing idea.

Nowadays, if you want a pop song to go viral on TikTok, it has to grab you within three or four seconds. And that's how lots of music spreads nowadays. I think with the death of literacy and the move into this more visual smartphone-based culture, we're moving from a culture that was much more able to handle nuance and complexity because it was rooted in literacy to one that is increasingly hostile to those things.

And, to use that point about the human experience of the world, if you're listening--there's a kind of--a long Bob Dylan song can paint you a picture of reality and its complexity and the complexity of human beings that is very hard to do if you have a two-minute-long, much less complex, much less rich song. There's room for both, but I just fear that we're losing more complex cultural forms.

Russ Roberts: Yeah. "Early one Sunday morning, I was laying in bed, wondering if she'd changed at all, or if her hair was still red," to pick one of the long ones.

James Marriott: On TikTok, you swipe past [inaudible 00:58:10], mid-harmonica solos. I don't think they would last on TikTok.

Russ Roberts: So, one of the other parts of the book we didn't talk about, which I very much appreciated, was the realization that this is not such a new phenomenon: that, we're focused on the smartphone, but television really was the beginning of the screen, the visual attractiveness of time sink for us, and that the remote control was the original scrolling. And I think that's very true. Anybody who has been in a hotel room late at night as I have, in the old days when you didn't have a cell phone and there were 200 channels on the TV, you just found yourself sometimes--I was going to say often--mindlessly scrolling across channels. I remember when I would complain about television--and I have a scene in one of my books where I really go off against TV, which is funny now because it's so unimportant relative to the cell phone--I remember telling my dad I was worried about the attractiveness of television. He said, 'Well, let's see how it holds up. Books have been around for centuries, and TV is 20 years old as a mass medium, maybe.' But, I think he should have been more worried.

I think there's an inevitability about this trend--that you're Sisyphus here: you're doing something that is unlikely to succeed. We're seeing a much longer trend that--reading is either going to be something--the people who can read, say, Henry James or Middlemarch by George Eliot; or who choose to--forget whether they can or they can't. People who choose to, it's going to be probably a pretty small number.

I don't know what that means for the future of the world. There is something incredibly sad about it to me, but I think that's a reality that's going to be unlikely to change. You can make all the arguments you want, 'Oh, this is going to be bad for democracy,' or 'Reading is really fun; you should try it.' It's a tough sell in our world, and I worry that that sell is just going to get even more and more difficult. So, I hate to be pessimistic, and I hate to end on such a pessimistic note. So, you got anything positive for me?

James Marriott: No. Well, I am by profession something of a pessimist and, unfortunately, by inclination and temperament. I think the point about TV is important because it reminds us that this is a long--I'm sure it is perhaps slightly this, but I hope it's more than just newspaper columnist comes along and yells about this very recent thing that's appeared in the world that's unsettling everybody, and actually we'll look back and think, 'Oh, that was just a flash in the pan. TikTok existed for 15 years and never moved on to something else.' We're living perhaps towards the end of a very long revolution in our culture that, as you say, begins with television, begins in the 1950s and 1960s. The first statistics for serious declines in reading come from the 1950s and 1960s.

And we are moving into a world in which these things are much less important. And that's a very long story. And, I think the length of the story should remind us of its seriousness. It's been happening for such a long time that this is not just something that, 'Oh, we'll just switch TikTok off.' 'Oh, we'll just get a handle on smartphones, and then it will be all right.' This is a very long-term trend in our culture, and I think that perhaps should make us a bit less hopeful. This is not a recent thing. This is a long direction that, very soon it'll be 100 years old.

I guess the argument I try and make at the end of my book--and your publisher always says, 'What about solutions? What's your solution to this problem?' And, you kind of think, 'Oh my God, I'm a horrible pessimist. What on earth have I got to say that's positive?'

The analogy that's often made, and I'm far from the first person to make that analogy, is between the rise of junk food and the culture of exercise in the 1960s and 1970s. So, McDonald's comes along; the world is flooded with burgers and chicken nuggets and chips; and a lot of people get much fatter. A smaller proportion of the population decide that they want to--they've understood that being healthy and skinny is no longer something that you can just do by absorbing the ambient nutrition environment around you; it's going to require effort. And these people begin to concentrate on working hard at their fitness. They start running marathons, they start going to the gym, they start lifting weights. And, people realize that physical fitness will require conscious effort.

And I kind of wonder--and I think probably this is already happening--is that in our current information environment, people will begin to decide that cognitive fitness will require a conscious effort, and that if we want to be cognitively fit, we can't just sit around absorbing the kind of informational junk food that's flying at us from every angle. We'll have to sit down and really concentrate on reading difficult books, exercising our brains. And, I think if there is a future for reading, it will be something that feels a lot more--to use a kind of horrible phrase--intentional and a lot less just like, 'I'm sitting at home or in the airport, I'm bored, what will I do? I will read a book because that's the most obvious entertainment available to me.'

I think it'll be much more: I want to read a book because I think this is a sort of experience that I value and that the world is not giving to me naturally. Therefore, I'm going to make sure that every evening I sit down for half an hour, an hour, to really try to really make sure that I read.

I mean, in some ways, I think that probably is the future of reading. In some ways, it's good that I think probably it does have some kind of future. I guess it does still make me sad that it has to be--I think it's slightly more artificial, and it will be less part of our inevitable lives in the way that it once was.

Russ Roberts: My guest today has been James Marriott. His book is The New Dark Ages. James, thanks for being part of EconTalk.

James Marriott: Thanks very much for having me.

title: Graph Technology Roundup – August 2026
description: The first in a series on the graph database ecosystem: a rush of new engines, LadybugDB's steady climb, DuckDB's graph moment, and Postgres 19 dropping property-graph support.
fullText:
The first in a series on the graph database ecosystem: a rush of new engines, LadybugDB's steady climb, DuckDB's graph moment, and Postgres 19 dropping property-graph support.

September 17, 2026 Christian Miles

Since starting the rankings in May we’ve seen some interesting changes and additions to the space. This is the first in a series of posts highlighting aspects of the ecosystem you may have missed.

GDB-Engines is the only resource online dedicated to tracking the facts and popularity of the graph database ecosystem. The core data is Open Source (PRs welcome!) and then augmented with our proprietary ranking analysis every month. This ranking is built from a blend of signals across the web to get a unique perspective on the key players in graph today.

Since starting the rankings the most obvious trend we’ve noticed is the explosion of folks building their own graph databases. It’s clear that the adoption and interest in AI tooling and knowledge infrastructures is directly influencing the graph landscape.

A common complaint we hear is “none of the databases out there were suitable for our needs” so folks make the jump to just building something themselves.

Whether this Snowflake mentality (not that Snowflake. And not like that) is the starting point for successful technology creation remains to be seen. Are they scratching their own itch with a tightly-scoped tool that does the job, or are these projects destined to be mothballed once the buzz from the LinkedIn announcement fades?

We also suspect the dominance of Neo4j in the graph ecosystem means that LLMs like ChatGPT and Claude are extremely familiar with the database and talking points. We suspect decades of folks discussing scaling needs and realities has been baked into the weights in a way that makes the models very comfortable with the idea of building your own Neo4j from scratch.

GDB-Engines was always intended to be exhaustive so we include any new database in good faith but will be assessing the activity and adoption of each to make sure we prune any abandoned or deprecated projects.

And the shape of these new entries is telling: six of the nine databases added this month are embedded, extensions or libraries. The new work is graph-as-a-feature, not graph-as-a-database.

We’ve heard from a few GDB fans that it’s been interesting to watch the steady rise of LadybugDB in the rankings. For the unfamiliar, LadybugDB is the de facto successor to KuzuDB after the project was deprecated following the acquisition by Apple last year. Arun Sharma has been relentlessly maintaining and innovating with the codebase, whilst tirelessly advocating for the use of Ladybug for modern AI workloads.

It’s therefore not surprising to see LadybugDB rise 3 places this month to #8 in the overall ranking.

Sharma’s a busy guy, here are three of his recent innovative projects building on Ladybug’s success:

DuckLabs (the company behind DuckDB) was acquired by AWS in August and we’ve seen an uptick in new graph projects based on the popular tooling. Duck RDF from Dan Bennett (S&P Global) and DuckGQL from Rahul Iyer (AWS) join the DuckPGQ community extension to give even more options for sticking with DuckDB for your graph workloads.

As the name suggests, DuckGQL leads with GQL as its query language - the Q, we can only assume, is for Quacking. And GQL is having a moment: the ISO standard now counts 18 engines on the board. Vendors like Ultipa are repositioning around it, and we expect AI coding assistants - which reach for well-documented standards over bespoke syntax - to push more teams the same way.

Get your product in front of thousands of high-intent technology specialists. Reach out to inquire about sponsoring GDB-Engines as we cover the graph technology landscape.

After lots of chatter and excitement for the inclusion of Property Graph support in Postgres 19, it appears that this has been dropped due to testing and quality concerns.

We added PostgreSQL SQL/PGQ to GDB-Engines in March to track the imminent release but looks like we’ll have to put this on ice. As an aside, it’s interesting that the news of the non-release of the feature appears to have been broken by an AI bot writing articles by hoovering up conversations from the pgsql-hackers mailing list. Whilst unsurprising, it’s a change that’s likely to influence the communication style of contributors, perhaps others will be less open with their announcements with the potential of a bot spinning professional communications into Breaking News.

We launched a new ranking last month for PostgreSQL graph extensions. Apache AGE remains at the top of the pack this month – this makes sense as it’s a solid project with years of use and support.

Some things about the graph landscape appear to be set in stone: Neo4j is sitting pretty at the top of the ranking and doesn’t appear to be threatened by any of the upstart AI approaches to building a graph backend. But the rest of the ranking is illuminating to see shift and develop over time. Interest in DuckDB, embedded architectures and the steady increase in standards adoption all show up as part of the story for GDB-Engines in August.

title: Hackers Actively Exploit Check Point VPN Flaw
description: Learn about the active exploitation of a critical VPN flaw in Check Point's Security Gateway and steps to secure your environment.
fullText:
Check Point is warning its users over the active exploitation of CVE-2026-85102, a severe vulnerability in its Security Gateway product. This critical pre-authentication remote code execution flaw exists in the VPNs certificate-handling functionality. According to BleepingComputer , Check Point released a security bulletin confirming that threat actors have been actively exploiting this gap to conduct unauthorized attacks.

What makes this even more alarming is the fact that attackers are exploiting it before users have the chance to patch it. The situation mirrors a wave of similar threats targeting other significant platforms and frameworks such as WordPress or Metas Muse AI assistant. Cybersecurity leaders in your organization need to take immediate action to protect against these growing threats.

Check Point Software Technologies disclosed a critical vulnerability in its Security Gateway product on 23 September. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-85102, is a pre-authentication remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability found in the VPN certificate-handling functionality. This means cybercriminals can exploit the flaw to execute arbitrary code on the server by sending specially crafted VPN certificates. The cybersecurity firm reports that threat actors have already started exploiting this flaw in the wild.

Check Point noted that exploitation is active. An earlier management server zero-day bug was detected by the company during an attack on July 23. That flaw was found in the Security Management Server, enabling unauthorized execution of scripts. Both vulnerabilities were swiftly patched the most recent exploit received its fix a day earlier on 23 September. The company advises all users to update their Security Gateway software immediately to the latest version.

The flaw is particularly serious because it allows attackers to execute malicious code on the targeted system. This can lead to a broad spectrum of malicious activities, such as data breaches, system hijacking, and unauthorized access to sensitive information.

The hackers exploit the vulnerability by sending customised VPN certificates to the impacted server. This action triggers the execution of malicious code without the need for user authentication. The critical nature of the flaw is underscored by its CVSS score of 9.8. This is on par with the severity of earlier bugs found in critical infrastructure such as the recent WordPress flaw (CVS-2026-87902), which allowed file manipulation for remote code execution.

Critical pre-authentication vulnerabilities in VPN software are especially alarming due to their potential for wide-scale exploitation. Check Point's advisory indicates that any device using the affected software is at risk if not patched. This makes prompt and coordinated response essential since these systems are often used for remote access and VPN setups.

Check Point Security's product portfolio is widely used in large enterprises, meaning this flaw puts a broad range of businesses at risk. In a report by BleedingComputer, Check Point has already documented active exploitation attempts.

Remote code execution vulnerabilities before user authentication are highly appealing targets for attackers. A flaw allows for the injection and execution of malicious code without the need for valid credentials, making it easier to infiltrate secure environments.

Businesses should prioritize this vulnerability because it can lead to significant data breaches and operational disruptions. The attacker can gain control over the server without any user interaction, making it difficult to detect and mitigate attacks early in the attack chain.

Another threat vector comes from the potential for lateral movement within a network. Once attackers gain access through a vulnerable VPN, they can spread to other connected systems. Security teams should be particularly cautious about network segmentation and access controls around VPN-enabled endpoints.

Check Point confirmed active exploitation of CVE-2026-85102, a critical vulnerability in its Security Gateway VPN. This finding has been reported by BleepingComputer.

The Hacker News further highlighted the risks of vulnerabilities in Check Point's systems, referring to past incidents including the exploit of a management server flaw. These instances illustrate broader system vulnerabilities.

The vulnerability, CVE-2026-85102, is a pre-authentication remote code execution (RCE) flaw in the VPN certificate-handling functionality.

Hackers are actively exploiting the flaw to gain unauthorized access and execute remote code on affected systems.

Organizations should apply the available fixes, monitor traffic closely, and assess the potential impact on their systems.

title: Moon Rabbit
fullText:
The Moon rabbit, Moon hare or Jade rabbit is a mythical figure in both East Asian and indigenous American folklore, based on interpretations that identify the dark markings on the near side of the Moon as a rabbit or hare. In East Asian mythology, the rabbit is seen as pounding with a mortar and pestle, but the contents of the mortar differ among Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese folklore. In Chinese folklore, the rabbit, Yutu, is often portrayed as a companion of the Moon goddess Chang'e, constantly pounding the elixir of life[1] for her and some show the making of cakes or rice cakes; but in Japanese and Korean versions, the rabbit is pounding the ingredients for mochi or tteok or some other type of rice cakes; in the Vietnamese version, the Moon rabbit often appears with Hằng Nga and Chú Cuội, and like the Chinese version, the Vietnamese Moon rabbit also pounding the elixir of immortality in the mortar. In some Chinese versions, the rabbit pounds medicine for the mortals and some include making of mooncakes. Moon folklore from certain Amerindian cultures of North America also has rabbit themes and characters.

An early Chinese source called the Chu Ci, a Western Han anthology of Chinese poems from the Warring States period, notes that along with a toad, there is a hare on the Moon who constantly pounds herbs for the immortals. This notion is supported by later texts, including the Song-era Taiping Imperial Reader. As rabbits were not yet introduced to China during Western Han, the original image was not a rabbit but a hare.[2]

Han dynasty poets call the hare on the Moon the "Jade Hare" (玉兔) or the "Gold Hare" (金兔), and these phrases were used often, in place of the word for the Moon. The famed Tang poet Li Bai, relates how "The rabbit in the moon pounds the medicine in vain" in his poem, "The Old Dust".[3]

In the Buddhist Jataka tales,[4] Tale 316 relates that a monkey, an otter, a jackal, and a rabbit resolved to practice charity on the day of the full moon (Uposatha), believing a demonstration of great virtue would earn a great reward. When an old man begged for food from them, the monkey gathered fruits from the trees and the otter collected fish, while the jackal found a lizard and a pot of milk-curd. Knowing only how to gather grass, the rabbit instead offered its own body by throwing itself into a fire the man had prepared. However, the rabbit was not burnt and the old man revealed that he was Śakra. Touched by the rabbit's virtue, he drew the likeness of the rabbit on the Moon for all to see. It is said the lunar image is still draped in the smoke that rose when the rabbit cast itself into the fire. The rabbit is believed to be a Bodhisattva.[citation needed]

A version of this story may be found in the Japanese anthology, Konjaku Monogatarishū, where the rabbit's companions are instead a fox and a monkey.[citation needed]

The Moon rabbit legend originated in China, and is popular and part of local folklore throughout Asia. It may be found in diverse cultures in China, Japan, India, Korea, Sri Lanka, Cambodia, Thailand, Vietnam, and Myanmar.[5][6][7]

This legend also gave rise to the Mid-Autumn Festivals of China, Tết Trung Thu of Vietnam, Tsukimi of Japan, and Chuseok of Korea, and Bon Om Touk in Cambodia, all of which celebrate the legend of the Moon rabbit. In Vietnamese mythology, the Jade Rabbit on the Moon is often accompanied by the Moon Lady and Cuội, who sits under a magical banyan. The trio has become the personifications of the holiday, when they descend to the mortal world and give out cellophane lanterns, mooncakes and gifts to children.[8]

In Journey to the West, when Tang Sanzang passes through India on his journey, a demoness wants to marry him so that she can absorb his yang essence and increase her powers. Sun Wukong sees through her disguise and fights with her. Just as Wukong is about to defeat the demoness, accompanied by the fairy Chang'e, Taiyin Xingjun descends on a colored cloud. The Monkey King hastily puts away his iron rod, saying, "Old Taiyin, where are you going? I, Sun Wukong, have been avoiding you." Taiyin replies, "The demon you are facing is the Jade Rabbit, who guards the mystical frost elixir in my Guanghan Palace. She secretly unlocked the jade gate and escaped from the palace, and it has been a year since then. I foresee she is currently in grave danger, so I have come to save her. I hope the Great Sage will spare her for my sake." Wukong reluctantly agrees, and Taiyin Xingjun takes the Jade Rabbit to the Moon and assigns her duties.[9][10]

Presumed to be arising likewise, through lunar pareidolia,[citation needed] legends of Moon rabbits also exist among some indigenous cultures of the Americas.

In ancient Maya art, glyphs, and inscriptions, a rabbit is frequently shown with the Moon Goddess[11] and another deity related to the Moon.[citation needed]

According to an Aztec legend, the god Quetzalcoatl, then living on Earth as a human, started on a journey and, after walking for a long time, became hungry and tired. With no food or water around, Quetzalcoatl believed that he would die until a rabbit grazing nearby offered herself as food to save his life. Quetzalcoatl, moved by the rabbit's noble offering, elevated her to the Moon before returning her to Earth, imprinting her image in the Moon. He told the rabbit, "You may be just a rabbit, but everyone will remember you; there is your image in light, for all people and for all times."[citation needed]

In Mesoamerican legend, Nanahuatzin and Tecciztecatl sacrificed themselves to become the sun and moon, respectively, during the creation of the fifth sun. Nanahuatzin did not hesitate to sacrifice himself, but Tecciztecatl hesitated four times before finally setting himself alight to become the Moon. Due to Tecciztecatl's cowardice, the other deities believed that the Moon should not be as bright as the Sun and threw a rabbit at Tecciztecatl's face to diminish his light.[12] Another version of the legend states that Tecciztecatl was in the form of a rabbit when he sacrificed himself to become the Moon, casting his shadow there.[citation needed]

In a Cree cultural legend, a young rabbit wished to ride the Moon, but only the crane was willing to take him there. The trip stretched the crane's legs, leaving them elongated. When the crane and the rabbit reached the Moon, the rabbit touched the crane with its bleeding paw, leaving a red patch on its head. In the present, all cranes retain the crane's long legs and red patch. According to the legend, on clear nights, Rabbit still may be seen riding the Moon.[citation needed]

fullText:
The new wearables come at a time of uncertainty for smart glasses, which are facing backlash over privacy concerns

Meta announced an advanced new set of virtual reality glasses and a collection of new smart glasses Wednesday, including an audio-only version without a camera.

At the firm’s Meta Connect conference in Menlo Park, California, executives said the new Ray-Ban Meta models set new standards for battery life and weight. They said the new glasses with screens in the lenses squeeze capabilities previously reserved for a full headset into a light set of spectacles that rest on a user’s ears.

The new wearables come at a time of uncertainty for the smart glasses category, which is broadly facing a backlash from sceptics and privacy campaigners around their ability to record video, frequently being dubbed “perv glasses” or “spy glasses”. Meta’s smart glasses are the most popular gadget in the category.

The Ray-Ban Meta Audio AI glasses seem tailored for the time. Lacking a camera, they may help avert some privacy worries, though Meta claims they have been in the works for several years. The glasses have microphones and speakers for music, calls and interacting with the company’s AI assistant, taking the recognizable form of Ray Ban’s Clubmaster or Burbank styles. The new versions are thinner and lighter than the camera versions and last up to 12 hours on battery and will cost £319 (€349/A$529).

The new Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 glasses, which do sport cameras, have longer battery life than their predecessors, lasting up to nine hours with support for Dolby Atmos audio. They will cost £409 (€449/A$679). Meta is also launching two new styles of its own-brand glasses in partnership with singer and actor Lisa. All of the firm’s smart glasses have an LED warning light that flashes when recording, but Meta said it has made improvements to its tampering detection, including during a livestream.

Finally, Meta is expanding availability of its Meta Ray-Ban Display smart glasses to outside the US for the first time since their announcement a year ago. The glasses with a virtual display in the right lens will go on sale in the UK and Canada from 23 September priced at £749 (CA$1,149) and will later expand to France, Germany and Italy on 13 October for €899.

The new Meta VR glasses are an evolution of the company’s pioneering Quest VR headsets, which have become some of the most popular on the market. But instead of being a bulky plastic headset, the 100g device is made of magnesium alloy and looks like an oversized set of glasses. The wearer peers through small lenses on to a 5K microOLED screen with a crisp 37 pixels per degree, making text look sharp and rivalling Apple’s high-end Vision Pro headset. Users can see out of the sides and through a camera system at the front for augmented reality features and awareness of their surroundings.

The glasses are tethered by a cable to a pocketable 300g puck containing the computing power and three-hour battery pack, which helps to remove the weight from a user’s head and makes the glasses five times lighter than the Quest 3 headsets, according to Meta.

The glasses are fully compatible with the vast Quest software library, but are designed for productivity and entertainment rather than games. The company described the glasses as “IMAX Enhanced” and supportive of 3D for movies. At launch, they will showcase a new Disney+ immersive experience that reflects landscapes from films such as Avengers: Infinity War surrounding a virtual cinema screen.

The glasses have the ability to display multiple virtual windows and to connect to a Mac or PC to mirror its displays. They have eye-tracking and hand-gesture control, including a virtual keyboard projected on to any desk or table, but also support Quest’s hand controllers or an Xbox game pad for games.

The Meta VR glasses will cost $1,299.99 and will be available from spring 2027 in North America, Europe and Asia.

fullText:
Prime minister says he told Sam Altman he was disappointed it had taken OpenAI ‘way too long’ to disclose breach

Anthony Albanese says an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June and the tech giant notified the government earlier this month using an email sent to a “public mailbox”.

Australia’s prime minister made the comments at the UN summit in New York, saying it appeared no personal information had been accessed in the AI breach.

Investigations assisted by the Australian Signals Directorate were ongoing into how the agent had infiltrated Australia’s government-run universal health care system, as well as three others.

They were the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the Victorian Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service Portal of Services Australia.

“This situation is obviously unacceptable,” Albanese said.

“Today, I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident and I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred.”

Albanese said both the delay and the manner in which OpenAI notified the government was disappointing.

“It took until 10 September before there was any notification at all. And the notification was an email sent to just the public mailbox,” Albanese said.

The email was sent to the public-facing email address publicdisclosures@servicesaustralia.gov.au . That inbox is checked once a day: the email was not read until 11 September.

Services Australia then reported the notification to the Australian Cyber Security Centre on 15 September.

A taskforce has been launched to explore the “legal situation” of the breach.

On Thursday, the NSW premier Chris Minns and the Victorian premier Ben Carroll both said Albanese had informed them the OpenAI breach had affected state websites – NSW’s crime agency and Victoria’s health department.

Both Minns and Carroll said it did not appear any personal information had been shared in the breach, though investigations were ongoing.

“New South Wales will be working with commonwealth intelligence agencies to get to the bottom of it,” Minns said.

Albanese said the OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access into the public-facing Medicare statistics reporting service portal, which is administered by Services Australia.

The portal contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics, such as spending.

Albanese said the agent had accessed “public and non-public files within the portal” and, in order to do this, “engaged in writing files as well to the internal server”.

The deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, said the government learned of the June breach “a couple of weeks ago” and ministers were informed last week.

Marles said the agent was non-human and he called the breach a “very serious incident”.

“What we have seen is unauthorised access in to an Australian government website and that is completely unacceptable and we have made that clear to OpenAI,” he said.

The AI agent had been given “a benign task” of researching health and medical statistics and, in doing so, had approached, as well as the Medicare portal, the three other Australian websites.

“In relation to those three, it interacted in a way that a member of the public might, so it only acted in an authorised way,” Marles told ABC radio on Thursday.

“But in relation to the medical portal of Services Australia, it sought information, information was not given, and then it effectively hacked into that medical portal and got that information anyway.

“It’s that unauthorised access which we are very concerned about. The impact is relatively minor, but the incident is very serious.”

Marles said the government had established a taskforce led by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet that was working with the Australian Signals Directorate and the AI Safety Institute.

“We will look at what is the legal situation in respect of this and what it means to have gained an unauthorised access, albeit in an unintended way,” the acting prime minister said.

“This is a warning about the fact that artificial intelligence, which is a technology that has huge opportunity to benefit humanity, has to be developed with enormous care. There have to be guardrails and safety measures in place which are way ahead of the capability which is being developed.”

The OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company was conducting an extensive review of “misaligned model activity during training and evaluation” and was “notifying third parties when our review identifies potential impacts to their systems”.

“During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation,” Pusateri said in a statement.

“In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend.”

He said the review had found aggregate health statistics and internal file names had been accessed but there was “no evidence of patient records being accessed”.

Pusateri said OpenAI was supporting investigations and that its review was ongoing, adding it was committed “sharing what we learn as that work continues”.

Lizzie O’Shea, spokesperson for Digital Rights Watch, said the fact it took three months for OpenAI to tell the government showed that there needed to be “basic rules and standards for tech companies”.

“Artificial intelligence has potential to do some things well, but it also poses huge risks – like hacking systems that store Australians’ sensitive personal data,” O’Shea said on Thursday.

“The question is whether governments are going to let AI and tech companies run wild or whether they, on behalf of ordinary people, will put rules in place for tech companies that will promote accountability and trust.”

Independent senator David Pocock said the OpenAI hack highlighted how slow the government had been to implement AI safeguards in high-risk settings.

Pocock criticised the government’s decision to shelve plans for a National AI Safety Act, and its dilatory approach to legislating new standards.

“We have these companies warning of existential threat and hacking critical government infrastructure and the Labor government’s response is ‘We’ll get to that next year’.

“There is also a big question here around why we aren’t holding these big tech companies liable for this kind of data breach. If it was an Australian who hacked the system they’d likely be heading for jail, yet there’s no accountability for AI companies developing this technology.”

Ed Santo, former human rights commissioner and co-founder of the Human Technology Institute, told ABC radio that Australians ought to “be worried”.

“This is the first time that this has happened in any major way to an Australian database, and it’s one of the most sensitive databases that we have in government.”

OpenAI had “instructed their AI agents to go looking for information about the public health system in Australia. When the AI agents couldn’t easily find that information, they decided to break the law,” Santo said.

Describing the behaviour as “misaligned model activity” was using “a very euphemistic term”, he said.

“If we were in the bricks and mortar world, if an employee of a company went and broke the law, particularly if it broke the criminal law, then that individual would suffer serious legal consequences, but so would their company. And so we need to make sure that that is true also in this era of AI.”

title: QuestDB (YC S20) Is Hiring a Sales Engineer

QuestDB is the low-latency time-series database on open formats. The engine is written in low-latency Java (zero-GC), Rust, C++ and assembly: columnar storage, vectorized and JIT-compiled SQL, streaming materialized views, and an open lakehouse tier on Parquet and Iceberg. Our open-source repository has passed 17k GitHub stars and we're the fastest-growing database in our category.
